content: Pneumonia is a common and potentially life-threatening condition. Corticosteroids have been proposed as a treatment option for various infections, but their specific role in managing pneumonia remains uncertain. This review updates a previous analysis published in 2011 and aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of corticosteroids in treating pneumonia. To conduct this review, researchers searched multiple databases, including the Cochrane Acute Respiratory Infections Group's Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and LILACS, as well as conference proceedings and trial registries, up to March 3, 2017. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared systemic corticosteroid therapy, used alongside antibiotics, to placebo or no corticosteroids in adults and children with pneumonia. A total of 17 RCTs involving 2264 participants were included in the analysis. Of these, 13 trials involved 1954 adults, and four trials involved 310 children. This update incorporated 12 new studies, excluded one previously included study, and excluded five new trials. One trial remains awaiting classification. All included trials focused on inpatients with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), with or without healthcare-associated pneumonia (HCAP). The risk of selection and attrition bias was generally assessed as low or unclear. Performance bias was rated as low in nine trials, unclear in one trial, and high in seven trials. Reporting bias was considered low in three trials and high in the remaining 14 trials. In adults with severe pneumonia, corticosteroids significantly reduced mortality (risk ratio [RR] 0.58, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.40 to 0.84; moderate-quality evidence). However, no significant reduction in mortality was observed in adults with non-severe pneumonia (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.45 to 2.00). Corticosteroids also significantly reduced early clinical failure rates (defined as death, radiographic progression, or clinical instability by days 5 to 8) in both severe and non-severe pneumonia cases (RR 0.32, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.70; and RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.83, respectively; high-quality evidence). Corticosteroid therapy shortened the time to clinical cure, reduced the length of hospital and intensive care unit stays, and decreased the risk of developing respiratory failure or shock not present at the onset of pneumonia. It also lowered the rates of pneumonia-related complications. In children with bacterial pneumonia, corticosteroids reduced early clinical failure rates (RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.70; high-quality evidence) based on two small, clinically heterogeneous trials. Corticosteroids also shortened the time to clinical cure in children. Hyperglycemia was significantly more common in adults treated with corticosteroids (RR 1.72, 95% CI 1.38 to 2.14). However, there were no significant differences between corticosteroid-treated individuals and controls in terms of other adverse events or secondary infections (RR 1.19, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.93). In conclusion, corticosteroid therapy reduced mortality and morbidity in adults with severe CAP, with a number needed to treat (NNT) of 18 patients (95% CI 12 to 49) to prevent one death. In adults and children with non-severe CAP, corticosteroids reduced morbidity but did not significantly impact mortality. While corticosteroid therapy was associated with an increased risk of hyperglycemia, the overall benefits appeared to outweigh the harms.
